https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘Where Washington is concerned, Andy Burnham shows no interest in performances of bonhomie with Donald Trump.’ Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen ‘Where Washington is concerned, Andy Burnham shows no interest in performances of bonhomie with Donald Trump.’ Photograph: Reuters Opinion Foreign policy The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s foreign policy: work in progress Editorial The prime minister has focused on domestic affairs since coming to office. But at a time of global disruption, he will need to define Britain’s place in the world Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.30 EDT Last modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.53 EDT Share A run of volatility in domestic British politics in recent years has tracked a period of global turbulence, and yet foreign policy over the same period has been an area of relative stability. What little is known about Andy Burnham’s approach to international relations expresses more continuity with Sir Keir Starmer’s administration than deviation. In negotiations with the EU, the red lines that prohibit membership of the single market or customs union still stand . Where Washington is concerned, Mr Burnham shows no interest in performances of bonhomie with Donald Trump, but his predecessor had already swapped that approach for a cooler pragmatic tone by the end of his tenure. The new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has opened a good dialogue with Marco Rubio , his US counterpart. Such is the density of integration in defence and security matters that incoming UK prime ministers, regardless of ideology, have little choice but to invest time in cultivating a bond with whoever sits in the White House. Anyone hoping for a spectacular transatlantic rupture and sudden clinch with Brussels will be disappointed. View image in fullscreen Ed Miliband and Marco Rubio. Photograph: Will Oliver/EPA Some patterns of consistency date back beyond the recent transfer of power within the Labour party to the previous Conservative administrations. Support for Ukraine in the face of Russian aggression was one of the few creditable positions taken by Boris Johnson , and that line has held through four transfers of power in Downing Street. The process of rebuilding functional relations with European neighbours predated the 2024 general election. Rishi Sunak negotiated the Windsor framework for Northern Ireland. He also ditched a bill that threatened chaos for businesses by vaporising retained EU laws without a timetable to replace them. The business secretary who executed that U-turn in defiance of the Tories’ fanatical Eurosceptic tendency was Kemi Badenoch . It was not a choice she highlighted in her subsequent bid to become Conservative leader. By then the party, relieved of the burden of governing responsibility, was in no mood to consider the merits of pragmatism where Europe was concerned. Having withdrawn to an ideological comfort zone, the Tories still cannot pretend that Brexit has been a success. Sir Keir became gradually more confident in attributing Britain’s economic woes to the terms of departure from the EU. But the shift was largely rhetorical because he was locked into a manifesto commitment that precluded a substantial change of direction. Mr Burnham has accepted the same constraint as a condition of his hand-me-down electoral mandate. Having accepted the parameters of Boris Johnson’s hard Brexit and acknowledged Britain’s security dependency on Washington, the prime minister doesn’t have much room to innovate in foreign policy. Nor has he shown much interest, focusing instead on domestic issues that are much more salient to voters than geopolitics. That is a rational priority for a new leader hoping to win over sceptical voters. But with no sign of global volatility abating, an international crisis will force itself on to Mr Burnham’s agenda soon enough. Global strife, especially when it whips up economic headwinds, quickly manifests itself as pressure to act in domestic politics. The prime minister has proved adept at connecting with an audience close to home. That advantage will be degraded if he cannot also connect his domestic agenda to a coherent strategy for engagement with the wider world. https://www.politico.eu/article/the-danu.text: Detonating a riverbed and sinking barges. Welcome to Europe’s increasingly desperate efforts to keep one of the continent’s most important waterways working. The Danube River reached dramatically low water levels this month, sending EU governments scrambling. Romanian authorities used explosives to steer more water toward the Cernavodă nuclear plant. The Hungarian government submerged vessels in a bid to keep water flowing past its own Paks nuclear plant. Some 180 tourists in Bulgaria had to be evacuated from a stranded ship near the port city of Vidin. There’s a lot at stake. The Danube, Europe’s second-longest waterway, is a vital artery for freight, drinking water, agriculture and industry. It helps cool major nuclear plants and feeds hydropower projects. The river basin stretches across 19 countries and supports tens of millions of people. But recurring drought, driven by climate change , threatens to change all that. Advertisement Advertisement “The prediction is that this will occur more often, and we need to look more systematically at water availability, water demands, and of course retention and resilience,” said Birgit Vogel, executive secretary for the International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River, which coordinates cooperation among countries across the basin. With drought becoming a recurring threat, Europe still doesn’t have a unified, binding policy to confront water shortages in the Danube and beyond. Responsibility remains split between national governments and river basin authorities, regulated by a patchwork of EU laws that green groups say are poorly enforced. Many of the bloc’s new resilience measures remain voluntary. Against that backdrop, national authorities are resorting to unilateral measures that, some argue, could wreak havoc on their neighbors and nearby ecosystems. Dimiter Koumanov, head of environmental protection at Bulgarian river NGO Balkanka, argues that countries are taking emergency action without considering the broader consequences. He is particularly concerned about the potential impact of such measures on Bulgaria’s drinking water. Danube countries are “doing everything they wish, and we in Bulgaria are paying the price,” he said. High stakes, low rivers “This summer has been another reminder that Europe is badly underprepared for climate change,” said Sara Johansson, water policy expert at the European Environmental Bureau. “Drying soils, degraded wetlands and destroyed ecosystems are turning landscapes into tinderboxes ready to ignite, while depleted rivers have exposed the vulnerability of our energy system.” Advertisement Advertisement The Hungarian Paks nuclear plant, which relies on the river for cooling, supplies around 40 percent of the country’s electricity, while Romania’s Cernavodă plant provides one-fifth of its power. When the river runs too low, governments aren’t just dealing with a water crisis — they also risk losing a major electricity source. This month Hungary began construction on a riverbed sill — a dam-like structure — to raise water levels around Paks. It’s a “potentially useful short-term intervention to raise water levels upstream,” said Tamás Gruber, head of WWF Hungary’s Living Rivers program. “However, the available information is not sufficient to assess its full ecological consequences or its effectiveness under future extreme low-flow conditions.” Such a structure could “worsen low-water conditions downstream and affect sediment transport, fish and other aquatic organisms,” he added. The controlled sinking of two barges takes place on the banks of the Danube River near the Paks nuclear plant in Hungary on Aug. 18, 2026. | Attila Kisbenedek/AFP via Getty Images Quick fixes to tackle the drought have largely remained national and fragmented across the seven EU member countries the Danube runs through, along with Serbia, Moldova and Ukraine. Organizations that coordinate the river’s management do exist, like Vogel’s ICPDR commission. ICPDR countries also have national agencies responsible for shipping, water management and environmental protection. These agencies cooperate on monitoring and navigation — but ultimately operate within their own national jurisdictions. Advertisement Advertisement Enter EU The EU’s Water Framework Directive requires member countries to protect and restore the bloc’s rivers, lakes and groundwaters, and to coordinate water management across river basins rather than solely along national borders. But experts and water sector groups say the EU has failed to deliver a coordinated policy response to improve drought preparedness, with dry summers set to become more frequent and intense. “The European Union is providing a framework. National governments can have a plan ... but most of the governance is done at the river basin level or at the local level,” said Loïc Charpentier, head of advocacy at lobby Water Europe. “That’s why you get this impression of, let’s say, non-coordinated action. You have some improvement to be done.” Last year a group of scientists issued a call for an EU Drought Directive to “harmonize and enforce risk management policies across the continent.” That was in response to the drought of 2022 . The event “affected most of the continent [but] our findings show significant regional disparities in management capacity,” they wrote . “In many countries — particularly those with agriculture-dominated economies — drought responses remain short-term and reactive, often leading to potentially maladaptive practices.” Brussels also unveiled a Water Resilience Strategy last year, containing some 50 measures to improve water security in the bloc. The strategy included a promise from the European Commission to give member countries technical guidance on how to draw up drought management plans — but those aren’t mandatory. A key EU nature law also commits the bloc to achieving 25,000 kilometers of free-flowing rivers in Europe by 2030, meaning those unhindered by artificial barriers such as hydropower dams — but again, it will be mostly “up to the member states how much they want to contribute [toward that goal],” WWF Austria river protection expert Marie Pfeiffer said. Advertisement Advertisement And as part of its ongoing mission to cut red tape and boost EU industry Brussels plans to revise the Water Framework Directive , with a focus on relaxing water protection rules for mining. Environmental NGOs warn the directive is already inconsistently enforced. Asked about the Danube drought, Environment Commissioner Jessika Roswall told POLITICO it’s “imperative to step up our preparedness across the board,” adding that the EU also needs to “evaluate whether our current EU water legislation remains fit for purpose from the angle of resilience, preparedness, water reuse and drought management” — hinting at the incoming revision. Gergely Patkó, an analyst for the Hungarian Water Utility Association, asserts that there’s “good cooperation between river basin authorities in different countries, and the Water Framework Directive supports this coordination.” Still, he warned that revising the directive could put more strain on drinking water during drought crises. Koumanov, the Bulgarian non-profit expert, said the best solution is to “follow the EU legal framework by the book and make it more stringent, aiming at better protection of the natural water resources, but I also know that this is Utopia for the moment. “Someday the wooden heads in the EU will learn the lesson and I hope that it will not be too late.”

Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre said it had extended the invitation in the hope of dismantling some of the barriers that kept Black children away from the pool. Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images Germany Scrapping of Berlin swimming day for Black children becomes latest in long list of race-linked pool rows Rightwing voices seize on plans to offer Black children an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool in the German capital Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent Mon 24 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 00.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It was meant to be an outing for Black children in Berlin and their families, offering them an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool set up by a local theatre. But the plans, slated for earlier this month, had to be scrapped after they were seized on by rightwing and conservative voices to whip up outrage, leaving organisers fending off racist emails and threats. Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre said it had extended the invitation in hopes of dismantling some of the barriers that would normally keep these children away from the pool. While other groups had similarly been invited to use pool exclusively without incident, the idea of Black children enjoying a private afternoon at a public pool proved to be controversial among some. “Berlin is a livable, diverse, colourful and free city. So why do we need safe spaces?” a local Christian Democrat politician, Aileen Weibeler, said on social media, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland co-leader Alice Weidel described it as “an apartheid” in which “white people are temporarily denied access”. It was the latest in a long list of incidents linking swimming pools to racism. Across North America and Europe swimming pools have often acted as a flashpoint for wider racial tensions and exclusions. View image in fullscreen Other groups had similarly been invited to use pool exclusively without incident. Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images Earlier this summer, an open-air swimming lake in the eastern German city of Halle made headlines after it refused entry to bathers who did not speak German. In the Netherlands, the Institute for Human Rights recently ruled against a pool after it was found to have singled out a Black child for an identity check. The list of incidents spans decades. In 2013, the Swiss town of Bremgarten moved to restrict asylum seekers’ access to swimming pools. In Bulgaria, Roma have sounded the alarm about being discriminated against at public pools, while in 2022, a swimming pool in Romania was fined just over €2,000 (£1,716) for barring entry to Romani children. View image in fullscreen Sibiu Aqua Park in Romania, which banned Romani children from entering. Photograph: Facebook Some of the association between racism and pools most likely comes down to the intimacy of these spaces, said Jeff Wiltse, the author of Contested Waters: A Social History of Swimming Pools in America. “They’re visually, physically, and socially intimate spaces, and I think that continues to pique people’s social anxieties,” he said. Wiltse has long studied pools in the US, recasting them as sites that reflect the wider tensions in society at any given time, from James Brock in 1964 pouring hydrochloric acid into a whites-only pool where Black men were swimming, to the Texas police officer who in 2015 pinned an unarmed Black teenager to the ground and drew his gun as he sought to break up a pool party. View image in fullscreen Motel manager James Brock dumps acid into a ‘whites only’ pool in Florida in 1964 after black and white demonstrators jumped in. Photograph: Rolls Press/Popperfoto/Getty Images In the US, “throughout much of the 20th century, swimming pools were homogenous spaces”, he said. “There was explicit racial segregation of public pools.” In the late 1940s, as public swimming pools in the US began to be racially desegregated, private pools began to spring up, particularly in suburbs that were almost exclusively white. Many people came to see swimming pools as “a certain type of social space in which the people there are all socially similar”, said Wiltse, who advocates tackling the issue by increasing public investment in community pools that could bring together people from different ethnic and racial backgrounds. The racialised history of pools – and its continued legacy today – has helped to give rise to a stark racial divide when it comes to swimming ability, one that has had deadly consequences. In the US, the fatal-drowning rate of Black and African American children is three times higher than that of white children. The statistics are even worse in England, where recent data found that children from Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities are 3.5 times more likely to drown than their white counterparts. Recent figures from Sport England suggest that 95% of Black adults and 80% of Black children do not swim at all. In 2022, Katrice Rodrigues set out to change this with the launch of Unity Swimming, a community organisation that runs weekly classes aimed at Black and Asian communities. “People get angry at that, saying: ‘How can it be inclusive if it’s just for Black and Asian communities?’” said Rodrigues, who is also a keynote speaker on diversity in aquatics. “My thing is that we’re making the whole of swimming more inclusive by creating these safe little spaces, which lead to more people swimming, and that makes swimming, as a whole, more inclusive.” The success of the programme has relied on Rodrigues and her team confronting the wide range of cultural barriers that keep minorities out of the pool, from having parents who are terrified of water to concerns over feeling out of place, dressing modestly or protecting Black hair. View image in fullscreen In 1952, 17-year-old Mamie Livingston (right) challenged racial segregation in Baltimore, Maryland, by seeking admission to a whites-only public swimming pool. Photograph: Afro-American Newspapers Archives and Research Center, Baltimore Other barriers have proven more enduring. “There’s a myth and a stereotype that Black people can’t float and can’t swim,” she said. “It’s not true, but I’ve had to correct two experienced swim teachers who thought that was a thing.” As summers become hotter across the globe, sending more people into rivers, lakes and pools in search of respite, the imperative has grown to ensure that as many people as possible know how to swim, said Rodrigues. “It’s the only sport that’s going to save lives,” she said. “If you’ve got water safety knowledge, you could help save someone else’s life as well as your own and your whole family. So this has a knock-off effect on families, on communities and for generations.” Explore more on these topics Germany Race Europe Swimming Inequality Social exclusion news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.investmentwatchblog.com/russ.text: Share this story The station is UVB-76. Folks call it The Buzzer. Also Doomsday Radio. Moscow never said what job it has. Most days it just buzzes on 4625. Then a man reads words plus numbers. Then the buzz comes back. The logs this week use NZhTI and TsZhAP ZMO9 and 65VU I8M7. Not Dimitry. That name is not in the list. On Aug. 24th morning it spoke four times in under two hours. Words were soap maker. Official. Blond. Shketoring. From 06:08 to 08:00 Moscow time. Then three quiet days. On Aug. 27th it woke up again. Early words were sub voice. Kumotom. Luftosil. Isoenzyme. Later chicken. Transgression. Zalochek. Moscow Times said the buzz broke 25 times that Thursday. TSN said busiest day in 20 months. Last time it went that wild was Feb. 12th 2025. Same day Trump and Putin talked on the phone. CIA boss Ratcliffe was in Moscow the day before. Papers glued the two things together. Nobody showed a paper that ties them. Same day they also read Dniester. Crime. Record. Same junk style as June 24th when it spat 20 messages. FLUSOBOB. Vurdalak. Kaloed. That mess. The June 24th burst sat next to Sikorski saying Russia might fake an attack then answer it. On July 31st the radio talked hours after a Russian missile landed in Poland. No ministry said these words mean launch. One write up even said there is no proof this is a nuclear event. People still call it EAM anyway.
